entities.name: The Rockefeller University
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Rockefeller University in New York City, founded in 1901 by John D. Rockefeller as the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, is the world's leading biomedical research institution and the first university in America dedicated exclusively to graduate education and biomedical research. Rockefeller's research has produced 40 Nobel Prizes — the highest Nobel density of any institution in the world per faculty member — including foundational discoveries in DNA structure, virology, cell biology, and immunology.

John D. Rockefeller founded the institute after his grandson died of scarlet fever, motivated by a desire to improve medical research and treatment. The institute's first director, Simon Flexner, established the model of full-time research faculty — at a time when American medical research was conducted by part-time practitioners — creating the template for academic medical centers. Alexis Carrel's 1912 Nobel Prize for vascular suturing and organ transplantation techniques at Rockefeller was among the institute's first major achievements.

Rockefeller's 40 Nobel laureates include: Oswald Avery (demonstrated DNA carries genetic information, 1944), Gunther Blobel (protein targeting, 1999), Torsten Wiesel (vision science, 1981), and David Baltimore (tumor viruses, 1975). The university's campus on Manhattan's Upper East Side overlooking the East River houses 70 laboratories. Rockefeller's per-faculty Nobel density — approximately 1 Nobel per 10 current faculty — is unmatched by any other institution, including Harvard, MIT, and Cambridge.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Rockefeller University's 40 Nobel Prizes per capita — the highest density of any institution in the world — and its discoveries in DNA structure, virology, and cell biology make it the single most productive biomedical research institution in human history.
